sections.heading: What the Preamble says

blocks.text: The Preamble is the introduction (preface) to the Constitution. It gives the summary or essence of the whole Constitution. The USA's Constitution was the first in the world to begin with a Preamble; India and many other countries followed this practice.

Present text: "WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation; IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION."

blocks.title: The four ingredients (components) of the Preamble
head: Ingredient
What the Preamble says
rows: The Constitution gets its authority from the people of India ("We, the people"). So the people are the chief source of political power in India.
India is a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic.

blocks.title: Order of words (asked often)
items: Nature of the State, in order: Sovereign, then Socialist, then Secular, then Democratic, then Republic.
Objectives, in order: Justice, then Liberty, then Equality, then Fraternity.
Justice is of three kinds: social, economic and political. (Religious justice and natural justice are NOT in the Preamble.)
Liberty has five kinds: thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.
Equality has two kinds: of status and of opportunity.
Fraternity assures two things: dignity of the individual, and unity and integrity of the Nation.

blocks.title: Words that are NOT in the Preamble (common trick options)
items: "Federal" is not there. The Preamble does not call India federal, unitary or quasi-federal. (Article 1 calls India a "Union of States".)
"Freedom" is not there. The word used is "Liberty".
'Economic liberty', 'political liberty' and 'liberty of occupation' are not there. In the Preamble, the words 'economic' and 'political' describe JUSTICE, not liberty.
"Unity" IS there (in "unity and integrity of the Nation").

sections.heading: Where it came from: dates and sources

items.what: Jawaharlal Nehru moves the Objectives Resolution in the Constituent Assembly
items.detail: It laid down the basic ideas and philosophy of the Constitution. It proclaimed India an "Independent Sovereign Republic".

items.what: Constituent Assembly adopts the Objectives Resolution
items.detail: Its modified form later became the Preamble.

items.what: The Constitution is adopted; this is the date written in the Preamble
items.detail: Some Articles came into force on this very day: citizenship (Art 5 to Art 9), elections (Art 324), the provisional Parliament, temporary and transitional provisions, and the short title. The others are Art 60, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393. The Emergency provisions and the appointment of judges did NOT start on this day.

items.what: Most of the Constitution comes into force. This is the 'date of commencement', celebrated as Republic Day
items.detail: On this day India was a "Sovereign Democratic Republic". It stopped being a British dominion.

items.what: The 42nd Amendment Act adds the words Socialist, Secular and Integrity
items.detail: The only amendment of the Preamble so far (as of Nov 2026).

blocks.title: How the Preamble was enacted
items: The Constituent Assembly enacted the Preamble AFTER the rest of the Constitution was enacted.
Reason: so that the Preamble would match the Constitution as finally adopted.
The President of the Constituent Assembly put the motion 'that the Preamble stands part of the Constitution' to vote, and it was adopted.

Apart from the Fundamental Rights, three other parts of the Constitution — the Preamble, the Directive Principles and the Fundamental Duties — also reflect the ideas of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948). (UPSC 2020 answer: all three.)

sections.heading: Nature of the Indian State: the five key words

head: Word
Meaning
Points to remember
rows: India is neither a dependency (colony) nor a dominion of any other nation. No authority is above it; it is free to run its internal and external affairs.

Being a member of the Commonwealth (declared in 1949) does not reduce India's sovereignty: the British Crown is only the symbolic head of the Commonwealth, and this was a declaration made outside the Constitution (extra-constitutional). India decides its own foreign policy. Membership of the United Nations (since 1945) also does not limit sovereignty. Because it is sovereign, India can acquire foreign territory, and can also give up (cede) part of its territory to a foreign state.
Added in 1976. Even before that, some Directive Principles already had socialist ideas; the 42nd Amendment only wrote the word down (made it explicit).

Indian socialism is 'democratic socialism', not 'communistic socialism' (where the State owns everything). It believes in a mixed economy: the public sector and the private sector exist side by side. It does NOT require the State to take over (nationalise) every means of production. It is a blend of Marxism and Gandhism, leaning towards Gandhian socialism. The Congress party adopted the goal of a 'socialistic pattern of society' at its Avadi session (1955). The New Economic Policy of 1991 (liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation) weakened (diluted) India's socialist character.
Added in 1976. All religions have the same status and support from the State. No religion is the official (state) religion.

India follows the POSITIVE concept of secularism: the State gives equal respect and equal protection to all religions. The Western (negative) concept means complete separation of religion and the State; it does not suit a country of many religions like India. In 1974 the Supreme Court said that even before the word 'secular' was added, the makers of the Constitution wanted a secular state; that is why Articles 25 to 28 (freedom of religion) exist.

Based on popular sovereignty: supreme power belongs to the people. The word 'democracy' comes from two Greek words: Demos (people) and Kratia (rule). Abraham Lincoln described democracy as 'government of the people, by the people, for the people'.

India has indirect (representative) parliamentary democracy: citizens elect representatives who make the laws, and the executive (ministers) is answerable to the legislature. Direct democracy, as in Switzerland, uses four tools: Referendum, Initiative, Recall and Plebiscite. Signs of Indian democracy: universal adult franchise (every adult can vote), periodic elections, rule of law, an independent judiciary and no discrimination. The word covers political, social and economic democracy.
The head of the State is elected (directly or indirectly) for a fixed period. He or she does not get the post by birth, as a king or queen does in a monarchy such as Britain.

India's head of State is the President, elected indirectly for 5 years (NOT the Prime Minister). 'Republic' also means: political power lies with the people, not with one person; there is no privileged class; and every public office is open to every citizen. It does NOT mean that every office (for example judges or officials) must be filled by election.

blocks.title: Secularism — provisions and cases
head: Item
Detail
rows: Preamble (the word 'secular'; liberty of belief, faith and worship); Art 14 (equality before law); Art 15 (no discrimination on the ground of religion); Art 16 (equal opportunity in public jobs); Art 25 (freedom of conscience and religion); Art 26 (religious groups manage their own religious affairs); Art 27 (no tax to promote any religion); Art 28 (no religious instruction in institutions run by the State); Art 29 and Art 30 (rights of minorities); Art 44 (Uniform Civil Code).
Equality applies to everyone — followers of every religion AND persons who follow no religion (atheists). So a statement that secularism is 'not applicable to irreligious persons' is wrong.
It does not mean the State has nothing to do with religion; it does not mean citizens will have no religion; it does not mean any religion is the state religion.
A nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court held that secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution.
The Constitution ended the old system of seats in legislatures reserved for particular religions (communal representation).

blocks.title: Socialism — court observations
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: D.S. Nakara case (judgment dated 17 December 1982; often written 1983, the year it was reported)

The Court said Indian socialism is a blend of Marxism and Gandhism, leaning towards Gandhian socialism. The basic aim of socialism is a decent standard of life for working people and social security 'from cradle to grave' (from birth to death).
Explains what 'socialist' in the Preamble means. (It was a case about government pensions.)
Democratic socialism aims to end poverty, ignorance, disease and inequality of opportunity.
Shows that socialism is about welfare, not about the State owning everything.

sections.heading: Objectives: Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity

head: Objective
Meaning
Provisions that give effect to it
rows: Equal treatment of all citizens without any distinction of caste, colour, race, religion, sex and so on; no special privileges for any section; and uplift of SCs, STs, OBCs and women. Example: removing caste discrimination.
No discrimination on economic grounds, and removing big gaps in wealth, income and property. Example: reducing income gaps.

Directive Principles, for example Art 39(b) and Art 39(c) (fair distribution of resources; wealth should not be concentrated in a few hands). So economic justice is found in the Preamble and in the Directive Principles.
Equal political rights, equal access to all political offices, and an equal voice in government. Example: an equal chance to take part in political life.
Art 325 and Art 326 (elections on the basis of adult suffrage, that is, every adult can vote)
Social justice and economic justice together are called distributive justice. Socialism provides for distributive justice.

Liberty means no restraints on what individuals do, along with opportunities to develop one's personality. The Preamble gives liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship. Liberty is not absolute (it is not a 'licence' to do anything one likes); it is qualified, that is, limited by the Constitution.
Art 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech and expression); Art 25 (belief, faith and worship)
No special privileges for any section, and equal opportunities for all. The Preamble gives equality of status and of opportunity. Equality has three dimensions: civic, political and economic.

Civic equality: Art 14, Art 15, Art 16, Art 17 and Art 18 (Art 18 abolishes titles, which gives equality of status). Political equality: Art 325 (no one can be left off the electoral roll because of religion, race, caste or sex) and Art 326 (adult suffrage). Economic equality: Art 39 (equal right to livelihood and equal pay for equal work for men and women).

A sense of brotherhood among all Indians. It assures two things: (1) the dignity of the individual and (2) the unity and integrity of the Nation. Fraternity is the principle in the Preamble that stresses national unity and integrity.
Single citizenship; the Fundamental Duties (Art 51A) on common brotherhood and the dignity of women; Art 1 calls India a 'Union of States', so states cannot break away (secede).

blocks.text: Do not mix up: "Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship" is the Preamble's wording; "Right to Freedom" is the heading over Articles 19–22 in Part III.

items: "Integrity" was added to "unity of the Nation" by the 42nd Amendment (1976), making it "unity and integrity of the Nation". Fraternity itself was there from the start; it was NOT added in 1976.
In 1949 fraternity already assured BOTH dignity of the individual and unity of the Nation — not dignity alone.
K.M. Munshi: "dignity of the individual" means the personality of every individual is sacred.

'Unity and integrity' covers both emotional (psychological) unity and territorial unity. It aims to overcome communalism, regionalism, casteism, linguism (division by language) and secessionism (wanting to break away).

Ambedkar (25 November 1949) said liberty, equality and fraternity form a 'union of trinity': separating any one from the other two defeats the purpose of democracy. Liberty without equality leads to the rule of a few over many; equality without liberty kills individual initiative. This is the 'trinity' of the Preamble.
So democracy is more than counting votes: the Preamble joins democratic government with justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.

sections.heading: Legal status: part of the Constitution? enforceable? amendable?

blocks.title: Cases
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: The Preamble shows the general purposes of the Constitution and is a key to the minds of its makers; it can help in understanding unclear Articles. BUT the Court said it is NOT a part of the Constitution.
The first view of the Supreme Court; it was later rejected.
Rejected the Berubari view: the Preamble IS a part of the Constitution. It can be amended under Article 368, but its basic features cannot be changed.
Linked the Preamble to the idea of basic structure (features Parliament cannot amend).
LIC of India case (1995) (LIC v Consumer Education and Research Centre)
The Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution.
Confirmed the Kesavananda view; it did not go back to the Berubari view.
Secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution.
Made 'secular' a part of the basic structure.
Dr Balram Singh v Union of India (25 Nov 2024)

Bench: Chief Justice of India Sanjiv Khanna and Justice Sanjay Kumar. Dismissed petitions challenging the addition of "Socialist" and "Secular" by the 42nd Amendment. The adoption date (26 Nov 1949) does NOT stop Parliament from amending the Preamble under Article 368. "Socialist" does not tie elected governments to any particular economic policy; India has a mixed economy. "Secular": the State neither supports nor penalises any faith; it is a basic feature. Challenging the amendment about 44 years later had no justification. The petitioners also argued that the amendment was passed during the Emergency by a Lok Sabha whose normal term had ended. The Court noted that Parliament had already discussed this point while considering the Bill that became the 44th Amendment Act, 1978, and it did not accept the challenge.
Latest ruling: both words are valid and stay (as of Nov 2026).

blocks.title: What the Preamble can and cannot do
head: Aspect
Position
rows: The founding fathers also voted it in as a part of the Constitution
It has no legal effect on its own, separately from the other parts
So it is wrong to say it has 'the same legal effect as any other part'
No — it does not give any power to the legislature
It is also not a limit (prohibition) on the legislature's powers
Courts cannot enforce it by itself as a right
It helps courts interpret unclear (ambiguous) provisions, including the scope of the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles
It cannot override provisions that are clear
Yes, under Article 368, but basic features cannot be changed
It cannot be changed by an executive (government) order, and it cannot be amended 'in any manner' Parliament likes

blocks.title: Basic structure
items: Basic structure means the features of the Constitution that Parliament cannot change using its amending power under Article 368 (Kesavananda Bharati 1973). This idea comes from court judgments, not from the text of the Constitution as it was in 1950.
Kesavananda Bharati: the basic elements of the Constitution are found in the Preamble; if they are removed, it is no longer the same Constitution.

blocks.title: The 42nd Amendment (1976)
items: It is the only amendment of the Preamble so far (only one time, as of Nov 2026). The Supreme Court held it valid.
'Sovereign Democratic Republic' became 'Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic': the two new words were put between 'Sovereign' and 'Democratic'.
'Unity of the Nation' became 'unity and integrity of the Nation'. So 'Integrity' is in the fraternity part, NOT in the description of India before 'Republic'.

It is called the 'Mini-Constitution' because it made a very large number of important changes: to the Preamble, the Seventh Schedule and many Articles. It also added Part IVA (Fundamental Duties) on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee.

sections.heading: Exam traps

items: The 42nd Amendment, 1976 (not 1979, and not the 44th) added Socialist, Secular and Integrity. Fraternity, Democratic, Republic and Sovereign were there from the start.
On 26 January 1950 India was a 'Sovereign Democratic Republic' — the words Socialist and Secular were not yet there.
Date in the Preamble: 26 November 1949 (adoption), not 26 January 1950 (commencement).
The Objectives Resolution was moved on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947. It was moved by Nehru (not Ambedkar, not Rajendra Prasad).
Republic means an elected President (head of State); it does not mean an elected Prime Minister.
Liberty is qualified (limited), not absolute. Justice came from the Russian Revolution; Liberty, Equality and Fraternity came from the French Revolution.
The Preamble does not contain 'Federal', 'Freedom' or 'economic liberty'. But 'Unity' IS there.
Berubari (1960): not a part. Kesavananda Bharati (1973): a part. LIC (1995): an integral part. It is a part of the Constitution, yet it is non-justiciable (not enforceable in court).

sections.heading: Article 1: India as a 'Union of States'

blocks.title: What Article 1 says
items: Article 1(1): "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States". The Constituent Assembly could not agree on one name, so it used both: India (modern name) and Bharat (traditional name).
Article 1 deals with two things: the name of the country and the type of polity (political system).
Part I of the Constitution (Union and its territory) has only Articles 1 to 4.
The names of all states and union territories (UTs) and their areas are listed in the First Schedule. So, to create a new state, the First Schedule must be changed.
India has a single citizenship. A state does not give its own separate citizenship. (See the Citizenship topic.)

blocks.title: Why 'Union of States' and not 'Federation of States' (Dr B.R. Ambedkar)
head: Reason
Meaning
rows: 1. Not the result of an agreement
The Indian federation was not formed by states signing an agreement to join (unlike the USA). So no state can break away by cancelling an agreement.
No state has the right to secede (break away) from India. The Union is indestructible (cannot be broken).
The country is one whole; it is divided into states only for convenience of administration.
blocks.note: Related view: the provinces of India were never sovereign states, before or under the Government of India Act 1935; powers were unitary, and the 1935 Act laid the base for Indian federalism. India is described as 'an indissoluble (unbreakable) Union of States'.

blocks.title: Acquiring foreign territory
items: As a sovereign country, India can acquire foreign territory in the ways recognised by international law: cession (by treaty, purchase, gift, lease or plebiscite), occupation (land with no recognised ruler), conquest or subjugation.

Once acquired, such territory becomes part of the territory of India (Article 1). The way it is acquired is decided by international law; that is a separate point, not the reason it becomes Indian territory.
Examples of territories acquired after 1950: Dadra and Nagar Haveli; Goa, Daman and Diu; Puducherry; Sikkim.

blocks.title: Sea and space limits (Maritime Zones Act, 1976)
head: Zone
Limit
India's power
rows: Full sovereignty, including the seabed, subsoil and the airspace above. Foreign ships (not warships) have a right of innocent passage (peaceful passing through).
Only sovereign rights over resources, not full territorial sovereignty
The Outer Space Treaty forbids any country from claiming (appropriating) outer space

sections.heading: Articles 2, 3 and 4: Parliament's power over states

head: Article
What it does

Parliament may by law admit into the Union, or establish, new states on terms and conditions it thinks fit

Laws under Art 2 and Art 3 may change the First Schedule (names and territories) and Fourth Schedule (Rajya Sabha seats), and make related (consequential) provisions, for example seats in Parliament and state legislatures. Art 4(2): such laws are NOT amendments of the Constitution under Art 368.

blocks.title: What Parliament can do under Article 3
items: Form a new state: by separating territory from a state, by uniting two or more states or parts of states, or by uniting any territory to a part of a state.

Article 3 does NOT list 'abolishing a state' as a separate power of its own. It also does NOT allow giving Indian territory to a foreign country; that needs a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
Explanation II (added by 18th Amendment 1966): the power to form a new state includes forming a new state or UT by uniting a part of a state or UT with another state or UT.

steps.step: President refers the Bill to the state legislature concerned
steps.detail: The state legislature gives its views within a time limit fixed by the President. The President may extend this time limit (a power added by the 5th Amendment, 1955). The Bill can be introduced only after this time limit is over.
The Bill can be introduced only with the President's prior recommendation, in either House of Parliament.

steps.step: Parliament passes it by simple majority
steps.detail: Ordinary law-making process. It is an ordinary (non-Money) Bill, so Article 108 joint sitting can be used if the Houses disagree, and the President can return it for reconsideration under Article 111.

steps.step: Views of the state are not binding
steps.detail: The President and Parliament may accept or reject the state's views, even if the views arrive in time. If Parliament changes the Bill, it need not be sent back to the state legislature again (Babulal Parate v State of Bombay, 1959).

blocks.title: Union Territories under Article 3
items: Explanation I (18th Amendment 1966): in clauses (a) to (e) of Art 3, 'State' includes a Union Territory.

But in the proviso (the part of Article 3 about asking the state legislature for its views), 'State' does NOT include a UT. So for a UT, the Bill need not be sent to its legislature; Parliament acts on its own.

sections.heading: How states were reorganised (1947–1956)

blocks.title: Integration of princely states
items: In 1947 there were two kinds of units: British provinces (under direct British rule) and princely states (ruled by Indian princes under British paramountcy, that is, the supreme control of the British Crown). The British interfered in a princely state's internal affairs only in special cases, such as to carry out Britain's international commitments.
Of 552 princely states, 549 joined India. Three refused at first, and were integrated later:
Hyderabad — police action (Operation Polo; began 13 Sept 1948, Nizam surrendered 17 Sept 1948).
Junagadh — referendum (plebiscite).
Jammu and Kashmir — Instrument of Accession.

blocks.title: What the 1956 changes did
items: The States Reorganisation Act and the 7th Amendment worked together.

The States Reorganisation Act 1956 also created five Zonal Councils (their meetings continue even now, for example the Eastern Zonal Council meeting in 2022).
Linguistic reorganisation in the 1950s is one cause of the rise of regional parties.

sections.heading: Exam traps

items: Article 1 says 'Union of States', NOT 'Federation of States'. 'Territory of India' is wider than 'Union of India'; UTs are in the Territory, not the Union.

sections.heading: What a Union Territory is, and the 8 UTs today

blocks.text: Under Article 1, India's territory has three parts: (a) States, (b) Union Territories, (c) territories India may acquire later. Today there are 28 States, 8 UTs and no acquired territories. States share power with the Centre (federal). UTs are under the direct control of the Central government, so they are also called 'centrally administered territories' — this is a clear unitary feature (power held by the Centre, not shared with the States).
The names and areas of all States and UTs are listed in the First Schedule of the Constitution.

blocks.title: Article 239 — the basic rule
items: Art 239(1): unless Parliament makes a law otherwise, every UT is run by the President, acting (as far as he thinks fit) through an Administrator appointed by him.
The Administrator is only an agent (representative) of the President. He is not a constitutional head like the Governor of a State.
The President decides the title: Lieutenant Governor, Chief Commissioner or Administrator.
Art 239(2): the President can appoint the Governor of a State as the Administrator of an adjoining (neighbouring) UT. Example: the Governor of Punjab is the Administrator of Chandigarh.
In that role the Governor acts independently of his own State's Council of Ministers — not on their advice.

The Ministry of Home Affairs is the nodal ministry for UTs, meaning the main ministry in charge. It handles their laws, finance, services (officers) and the appointment of Lieutenant Governors and Administrators.

blocks.title: Parliament's power over UTs
items: Parliament can make laws on any subject of all three lists (Union, State, Concurrent) for UTs.
This power continues even for Puducherry, Delhi and J&K, which have their own legislatures. Their legislatures do not reduce the control of the President and Parliament.

blocks.title: Article 240 — President's regulations
items: The President can make regulations for the 'peace, progress and good government' of: Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, and Ladakh.
For Puducherry, the President can make such regulations only when its Assembly is suspended or dissolved — not while it is functioning.
Chandigarh is not in this list.
A regulation has the same force as an Act of Parliament. It can even repeal (cancel) or amend (change) an Act of Parliament as it applies to that UT.

blocks.title: Advisory committees (UTs without legislature)
items: The five UTs without a legislature (Andaman and Nicobar, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Lakshadweep, Ladakh) have a Home Minister's Advisory Committee (chaired by the Union Home Minister) or an Administrator's Advisory Committee (chaired by the Administrator).
Members include the UT's Members of Parliament and elected local body members.

blocks.title: UTs in Parliament
items: Lok Sabha (Art 81): at most 530 members from States and at most 20 from UTs (maximum strength 550).
UT members of Lok Sabha are chosen by direct election under the Union Territories (Direct Election to the House of the People) Act, 1965.
Rajya Sabha: only 3 UTs are represented — Delhi, Puducherry and J&K. The other five have too small a population.

blocks.title: Puducherry — Article 239A
items: Art 239A was added by the 14th Amendment Act, 1962.
It lets Parliament, by law, create for Puducherry a legislature, or a Council of Ministers, or both.

Art 239A(2): such a law is NOT treated as an amendment of the Constitution under Article 368 (the special amendment procedure), even if it changes or affects the Constitution. So an ordinary Act of Parliament is enough.
Using this, Parliament passed the Government of Union Territories Act, 1963. Puducherry's Assembly and Council of Ministers work under this Act.
Puducherry Assembly: 30 members. It can make laws on any subject of the State List and the Concurrent List.

blocks.title: Ordinances — Article 239B
items: The Administrator can issue an Ordinance when the legislature is not in session.
But only after getting instructions from the President.
The Ordinance ends six weeks after the legislature meets again, or earlier if the legislature passes a resolution rejecting it.
No Ordinance can be issued while the legislature is dissolved or suspended.
Art 239AA(8): the same Article 239B rules also apply to Delhi — there, the Lieutenant Governor issues the Ordinance and the Delhi Assembly is the legislature.

sections.heading: Delhi: Art 239AA, 239AB, court cases and the 2021/2023 laws

blocks.title: 69th Amendment Act, 1991 (Art 239AA and 239AB)
items: Gave Delhi a special status and renamed it the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi; in force from 1 Feb 1992.
Its Administrator is called the Lieutenant Governor (LG).
Created a Legislative Assembly of 70 members, directly elected; elections are held by the Election Commission of India.
The Assembly can make laws on all State List and Concurrent List matters, except three State List matters: public order, police and land.
But Parliament's laws prevail over the Assembly's laws. Parliament does NOT lose its power even after the Assembly makes a law on a State List matter.
Council of Ministers: at most 10% of Assembly strength = 7 (Chief Minister and 6 ministers).

The Chief Minister is appointed by the President (not by the LG). Other ministers are appointed by the President on the Chief Minister's advice. They hold office during the pleasure of the President (the President can remove them at any time).
The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Assembly (all ministers together must keep the Assembly's support).
This did NOT make Delhi a full State.

blocks.title: LG vs ministers — Article 239AA(4)
items: The Council of Ministers gives 'aid and advice' to the Lieutenant Governor (LG), and the LG normally acts on it. The exception is matters where the law lets the LG act in his own discretion (own judgement).
If the LG and a Minister differ, the LG refers the matter to the President, and acts as the President decides.
If the matter is urgent, the LG can take immediate action until the President decides.

blocks.title: Article 239AB — failure of machinery in Delhi
items: If Delhi cannot be governed according to Art 239AA, the President can suspend those provisions, either on the LG's report or on his own information. This works like President's Rule in a State.
Article 356 is NOT used, because Art 356 is for States, and Delhi is still a UT even though it has an Assembly.

blocks.title: Single citizenship
items: India has a federal set-up (Centre and states) but only ONE citizenship: Indian citizenship. Citizens owe loyalty only to the Union. There is no separate state citizenship.
India copied single citizenship from Canada.

USA and Australia have dual (double) citizenship: a person is a citizen of the country AND of the state (constituent unit) where he or she lives. Two sets of rights; a state can favour its own citizens.
Art 1 calls India a 'Union of States', but states do not give any citizenship of their own.
Purpose: equal rights everywhere, fraternity and national unity.
In India, both a citizen by birth and a naturalised citizen can become President. In USA, only a citizen by birth can.
Single citizenship is a feature of the Constitution; 'dual citizenship' is NOT.

sections.heading: Constitution: Articles 5 to 11 (Part II)

blocks.text: Part II (Art 5 to 11) only says who became a citizen at the start of the Constitution (26 January 1950). It does not say how citizenship is gained or lost later. It leaves that to Parliament, which made the Citizenship Act, 1955.

blocks.title: Articles at a glance
head: Article
Subject
Key detail
rows: Citizenship at the commencement (start) of the Constitution
Domicile (permanent home) in India is a MUST, plus any ONE of three: (a) born in India, or (b) either parent born in India, or (c) ordinarily resident in India for 5 years just before commencement
Persons who migrated to India from Pakistan

The person, or either parent, or any grandparent, was born in India as defined in the Government of India Act 1935 (undivided India). Came BEFORE 19 July 1948: must have lived in India ordinarily since migration. Came ON or AFTER 19 July 1948: must be registered by an officer appointed by the Government of the Dominion of India, on an application made before commencement, after 6 months' residence just before applying. (19 July 1948 = date the permit system for migration started.)
Persons who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947

Main rule: they are NOT citizens. Exception: those who came back under a permit for resettlement or permanent return issued by lawful authority are treated like Art 6 later migrants (need registration after 6 months' residence). Covers migration between 1 March 1947 and 26 January 1950.
Persons of Indian origin living outside India

The person, or either parent, or any grandparent, was born in India as defined in the original Government of India Act 1935 (a great-grandparent does not count). Must be registered by India's diplomatic or consular representative in the country where he lives, before OR after commencement. Residence 'outside India' also uses the 1935 Act definition.
Such a person is not a citizen under Art 5, nor deemed a citizen under Art 6 or Art 8. This is the basis of the rule that India does not allow dual citizenship.
Continuance of the rights of citizenship
A citizen continues to be one, subject to any law made by Parliament (so Parliament's power under Art 11 remains)
Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law
Parliament has full (plenary) power over acquisition, termination and all other citizenship matters

blocks.title: Important connected facts
items: Art 5 to Art 9 (citizenship), with elections, provisional Parliament and temporary provisions, came into force on 26 November 1949 itself, under Art 394. The rest came into force on 26 January 1950.
Art 393 gives the short title 'Constitution of India'; Art 395 repealed the Indian Independence Act 1947 and the Government of India Act 1935.
A law under Art 11 is an ordinary law. It is passed by simple majority, and is NOT an amendment of the Constitution under Art 368.
Citizenship is in the Union List (Entry 17), so only Parliament can make citizenship laws, not the Union Cabinet, the Supreme Court or state legislatures.
The Constituent Assembly's Ad-hoc Committee on Citizenship was headed by S. Varadachari (he was not a member of the Assembly).

sections.heading: Citizenship Act 1955: five ways to become a citizen

blocks.text: The Citizenship Act, 1955 (passed by Parliament in 1955, under Art 11) deals with getting and losing citizenship after 26 January 1950. It is run by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), which decides registration and naturalisation applications. It originally had 'Commonwealth Citizenship' (special status for citizens of Commonwealth member countries), which the 2003 amendment removed. Adoption, owning land or property, depositing money, or ethnic identity are NOT ways to become a citizen.

Main condition
rows: Born in India; conditions depend on date of birth (table below)
Born outside India to an Indian citizen parent (table below)
Only the categories listed below. The person must not be an illegal migrant (a foreigner who entered without valid papers, or stayed beyond the permitted time). Must take an oath of allegiance.
A foreigner who has lived in India for a long time and meets the qualifications in the Third Schedule of the Act. Must take an oath of allegiance.

When a foreign territory becomes part of India, the Central Government by notified order (in the Official Gazette) says which people of that territory become citizens and from which date. Example: Citizenship (Pondicherry) Order 1962.

sections.heading: Losing citizenship: renunciation, termination, deprivation

blocks.title: Three ways (apply to citizens under the Act or the Constitution)
head: Way (Section)
How it works
Special points
rows: An adult citizen of full capacity makes a declaration; citizenship ends when it is registered

In a war involving India, registration is withheld until the Central Government directs. The person's minor children also lose citizenship; each can resume it by a declaration within 1 year after turning 18.
Voluntarily (knowingly, without force) acquiring another country's citizenship ends Indian citizenship automatically; no separate order needed
Does not apply during a war in which India is engaged. Involuntary acquisition does not count.
Deprivation (Section 10) — compulsory, by Central Government order

Grounds: (1) registration or naturalisation got by fraud, false statement or hiding a material fact; (2) disloyalty or disaffection to the Constitution by act or speech; (3) unlawful trade or contact with an enemy during war; (4) imprisoned for 2 years in any country within 5 years of registration or naturalisation; (5) ordinarily resident outside India for 7 years continuously

Applies to citizens by registration or naturalisation, and to those who became citizens at the start only under Art 5(c) (5 years' residence). The Government must also be satisfied that letting the person stay a citizen is not for the public good. Before the order, the Government must give written notice of the ground. The person can ask for the case to be sent to a Committee of Inquiry (a chairman with judicial experience and two other members), except when the ground is 7 years' residence abroad.
